title: One Van, Two Routes
story: Two couriers deliver along the same long street. Each one's stops are stored as a chain: every stop points to the next one, and each chain is already sorted by the stop's position along the street, in metres from the depot.
One courier calls in sick, so a single van must do both rounds in one drive down the street. The dispatcher needs one chain with every stop from both routes, still sorted by distance.
task: Write mergeRoutes(first, second). Both arguments are sorted linked lists (smallest distance first; null / None means no stops). Return the head of one sorted list that contains every node of both.
If both routes have a stop at the same distance, keep both stops. Reuse the existing nodes by relinking them rather than creating new ones.
constraints: -100,000 ≤ distance ≤ 100,000 (negative means west of the depot)
Each route is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: Compare the first stops: 2 beats 3, so 2 goes first. Then 3 beats 5, then the two 5s (both kept), then 9 beats 12, and finally the 12 that is left over.
The first courier had no stops, so the van just follows the second route.

hints: Look only at the first stop of each route. Which of the two must be the very first stop of the merged route?
The smaller of the two front stops goes first. Take it off its route. Now you have the same question again with one stop fewer.
Keep a tail pointer to the last stop of the merged route so you can attach the next one in O(1). A dummy starting node saves you from treating the first attachment as a special case.

Create a dummy node and set tail = dummy. While both routes have stops, attach the smaller front node to tail.next, advance that route and advance tail. When one route runs out, attach the rest of the other in one step. Return dummy.next.
bruteForce: Copy every distance from both chains into an array, sort it, and build a new chain from it.

The sort costs O((n + m) log(n + m)) and throws away the fact that both routes were already sorted. It also allocates a whole new chain. Merging walks each route once, O(n + m), and reuses the nodes you already have.

walkthrough: The first stop of the merged route must be the smaller of the two front stops. After you take it, the same reasoning applies to what is left. So you repeatedly compare two fronts and move the smaller one to the end of the result.
• Fronts 5 and 5. Equal, take the first route's 5. Result: … → 3 → 5.
• Fronts 9 and 12. Attach 9. The first route is now empty.
• Attach what is left of the second route, 12, in one step. Return dummy.next: 2 → 3 → 5 → 5 → 9 → 12.
The dummy node means you never need an if for "is the result still empty?". Without it, the first attachment needs special code, and that is where bugs hide.
solution.timeWhy: n and m are the two route lengths. Each step attaches one node, and every node is attached once.
solution.spaceWhy: The nodes are relinked, not copied. Only the dummy and a few pointers are extra.
solution.takeaway: To combine two sorted sequences, repeatedly take the smaller front item. Use a dummy head and a tail pointer whenever you build a linked list node by node. This merge step is the heart of merge sort.
